name: English Reformation
notes: Break with Rome and establishment of a national church in England.
summary: A sequence of political and religious changes that separated English church government from Rome and transformed worship and doctrine.
formation_narrative: Henry VIII’s dispute over his marriage coincided with a struggle over jurisdiction and royal power. Parliamentary acts in the 1530s transferred authority from Rome to the crown. Further Protestant reform, Catholic restoration, and Elizabethan settlement followed under successive monarchs. The process cannot be reduced to one fully Protestant church springing into existence in 1534: political separation and doctrinal reform proceeded at different speeds.
core_beliefs: Authority was contested: royal supremacy replaced papal jurisdiction before every doctrinal question was settled.
Protestant teaching developed: later articles and vernacular worship expressed reform beyond the initial constitutional break.
No single movement creed: the participants’ aims differed across reigns; the later Anglican settlement is one outcome of the process.

key_figures.name: Henry VIII
key_figures.summary: The English monarch whose marital and jurisdictional conflict with Rome led to royal supremacy; his political break did not immediately settle all later Protestant doctrine.

key_figures.name: Thomas Cromwell
key_figures.role: minister who steered the parliamentary break
key_figures.summary: Henry VIII’s minister who helped steer the parliamentary measures transferring English ecclesiastical authority away from Rome.

key_figures.name: Thomas Cranmer
key_figures.role: archbishop central to later prayer-book reform
key_figures.summary: The English archbishop whose liturgical work helped make common prayer a central expression of reformed English Christianity.

key_documents.title: Act of Supremacy
key_documents.significance: A jurisdictional statute defining royal headship, not a complete Protestant confession.

key_documents.title: Thirty-nine Articles
key_documents.significance: Later Anglican doctrinal settlement; it should not be projected unchanged onto Henry’s initial break.

profile_scope: This is an introductory profile. It distinguishes shared teaching from historical development; sources do not imply that every member held an identical position. No formal corporate dissolution is asserted for this historical process. The status is unknown at the institutional level; the ending narrative explains its diffusion or development.
ending_narrative: The process passed through Protestant reform, Catholic restoration, and later Anglican settlement rather than ending in one formal dissolution. Its institutional and theological consequences continue in the Church of England and wider traditions. The Church of England link is a principal outcome, not proof that every reforming participant intended the same result.

name: Church of England
notes: Established as the English national church in the Reformation era.
summary: England’s established church, shaped by ancient Christian continuity, the Reformation, and a shared liturgical and episcopal inheritance.
formation_narrative: The Reformation separated English church authority from Rome through royal and parliamentary action. Subsequent settlements established a distinctive combination of Reformed teaching, common prayer, and historic episcopal ministry. The church’s own doctrinal canons identify Scripture, the Articles, prayer book, and Ordinal as guiding sources. Its members have differed substantially in churchmanship, and the 1534 marker should be explained as a jurisdictional break rather than the beginning of Christianity in England.
core_beliefs: Scripture and creeds: biblical teaching is read within the inherited Christian tradition.
Common prayer and sacraments: worship is shaped by authorized liturgy, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper.
Episcopal and national structure: bishops and parishes organize an established church whose internal traditions include evangelical, catholic, and broad-church emphases.

ending_narrative: The Church of England continues as England’s established church. American Anglican organization and later Methodist or Separatist developments did not terminate it. Those are related histories and departures, not terminal successors to a vanished parent.
